The mean (or average) for a set of numerical values X, is the sum of these values 
divided by their number. The mean value is often dencted by a bar above the 
value symbol:

The range of values in a set is the difference between the maximum and 
minimum values. For example, the range of values inthe set (2, 3, 7)is 7 -2 = 5. 
Scientific notation 
Scientific notation is the standard way of representing numbers of various 
magnitudes. For example, the value 3.5 x 108 is the same as 3500000. The 
mantissa 3.5 shows all significant figures in the value while the exponent 108 
shows the magnitude of the value. In scientific notation, the mantissa must 
be equal to or greater than 1 but less than 10, and the exponent must have an 
integer (whole-number) value. 
The order of magnitude for a particular value is the nearest power of 10 
representing that value. To determine the order of magnitude, any mantissa of 
less than 5 is rounded down to 1, and a mantissa of 5 or greater is rounded up 
to 10. The result is then represented using scientific notation, and the exponent 
(without the mantissa) gives the order of magnitude (table 2).

Approximation and estimation 
In many practical situations, the exact value of the measured or calculated 
quantity is not required, so it can be estimated using the results of similar 
measurements or determined approximately by ignoring the effects of certain

3.1 Applying general mathematics 
factors. For example, the enthalpy change for a particular reaction can be 
estimated using the average values of bond enthalpies (Reactivity 1.2), and 
the intermolecular forces between gas molecules can be ignored when a real 
gas is described using the ideal gas model (Structure 1.5). Both estimation and 
approximation are very powerful technigues that can greatly simplify calculations 
and provide practically important results that would be impossible to obtain 
otherwise. However, these techniques must be used with care to ensure that the 
ignored factors do not introduce unacceptably large errors or uncertainties. 
Proportionality and correlation 
Direct proportionality is the relationship between two variables x and y that can 
be represented by the linear function y = ax, where a = 0 is the proporticnality 
constant. The statement “y is directly proportional to x” means that the ratio of 
yto xis constant: when x doubles, y also doubles, and so on. In the Einstein 
equation, E = mc?, the values of E and m are directly proportional, and the 
proportionality constant is ¢2. 
Inverse proportionality is represented by the functiony = —?C-, wherea=0. In 
this relationship, an increase of xby a certain factor decreases yby the same 
factor. In the ideal gas equation, pV =nRT, the values of p and V are inversely 
proportional to each other. 
Correlation is the degree to which a pair of variables are linearly related to 
each other. The correlation is said to be positive when both variables change 
in the same direction: when one variable increases, the other also increases, 
and when one decreases, the other also decreases. In contrast, the correlation 
is negative when the two variables change in opposite directions: when one 
increases, the other decreases, and vice versa. The closer the relationship 
between the two variables is to proportionality (either direct or inverse), the 
stronger the correlation (figure 28). 
Assessment tip 
The strength of correlation is characterized quantitatively by the correlation 
coefficient (R), which can take any value between O and 1 for a positive 
correlation or between -1 and O for a negative correlation. The greater 
the absolute value (modulus) of R, the stronger the correlation. IFR =0, no 
correlation is observed. 
The concepts of correlation strength and correlation coefficient are not 
assessed in examination papers, but they might be used for processing 
experimental data in your internal assessment. 
The square of the correlation coefficient, known as the coefficient of 
determination (R?, characterizes the predictive power of a graphical 
relationship, which will be discussed in Tool 3.3.

Generally, percentage error characterizes the magnitude of systematic error(s) 
and thus the accuracy of the obtained result: the greater the percentage error, 
the further the measured or calculated value is from the true value. 
Percentage uncertainty shows the ratio of the absolute uncertainty (u) of the

Percentage uncertainty characterizes the magnitude of random errors and thus

lower the precision of that value. 
Absolute, relative and percentage uncertainties will be discussed in

3.2 Using units, symbols and numerical values 
Continuous and discrete variables 
A continuous variable can take any value within a certain range. For example, 
the concentration of sulfuric acid in an aqueous solution can vary from O to Assessment tip 
100%, and the number of possible values for this (and any other) concentration 
is infinite. With the exception of amount of substance, all base S| quantities Generally, the values for 
(time, length, mass, electric current, temperature and luminous intensity) are continuous variables are 
continuous, and so are all variables derived from these quantities, such as determined by measurement 
density or electric potential difference. while the values for discrete 
variables are determined by 
counting. Amount of substance 
(in moles) is usually treated as 
a continuous variable although 
the exact number of molecules 
or other structural units in a very 
small sample can be determined 
by counting. 
Discrete variables can take only a limited number of values within any given 
range. For example, the number of carbon atoms in an organic compound 
can take only integer values (1, 2, 3 and so on), although the total number 
of these atoms in a molecule has no upper limit. Other examples of discrete 
variables are the number of electrons in an atom, quantum numbers describing 
the states of these electrons, the number of chemical elements present in the 
analysed sample and the number of trials in a particular experiment. 
In graphical form, continuous variables are often represented by scatter 
plots while discrete variables should be shown as line graphs or bar 
charts (Tool 3.4).

numerical values

International System of Units (SI) 
The International System of Units (S, from the French Systeme International 
d'Unités) is the most commonly used system of measurement. Its building 
blocks are the seven base units: length (metre, m), mass (kilogram, kg), time 
(second, s), electric current (ampere, A), temperature (kelvin, K), amount 
of substance (mole, mol) and luminous intensity (candela, cd). All other 
units, such as those of volume (m?), density (kgm=3), energy (joule, |, where 
1) =1kgm?s~?) and so on, are derived from the seven base units. 
The use of universal and precisely defined units is very important, as it % 
allows scientists from different countries to understand one another and Decimal prefixes and unit

Significant figures 
Any measurement involves uncertainty (Tool 3.3), which limits the precision of 
the measured value. This uncertainty is reflected in the number of significant 
figures (sf) used to express any numerical value obtained by measurement 
or calculated from experimental results. For example, the length of asmall 
object measured with a ruler typically has no more than three sf (see figure 7 
in Tool 1.2). The last sfin a length measurement can never be obtained with 
certainty but only estimated, depending on the position of the measured 
object between two adjacent scale divisions. 
In figure 29, the measured length is 3.67 cm. The first two figures, 3 and 6, are 
certain, as the length is greater than 3.6 but less than 3.7 cm. The last figure, 7, 
is uncertain, as the actual length could be 3.66 or 3.68cm.

A decimal place is the position of adigit after the decimal point. If the last one 
or more decimal places in a number are zeros, they must never be omitted, 
as they represent significant figures. For example, if a digital balance displays 
the mass of a sample as 2.500 g, this mass must be recorded as shown rather 
than 2.5g. The loss of trailing zeros reduces the precision of the measurement, 
which in turn might reduce the precision of all other numerical values derived 
from this measurement (e.g. the amount of substance or density of the sample). 
214

3.3 Processing uncertainties 
In calculations, the number of significant figures in the final result is determined 
according to the following rules. 
+ Addition or subtraction: the result has the same number of decimal 
places as the argument (given numerical value) with the smallest number of 
decimal places. For example, 1.234 + 2.0 = 3.2 (one decimal place). 
¢ Multiplication or division: the result has the same number of sfas the 
argument with the smallest number of sf. 
Forexample, 1.234 x 2.0 = 2.5 (two sf). 
* Exponent or root: the result has the same number of significant figures as the 
argument. For example, 1.234% = 1.523 and 4/1.234 = 1.111 (four sf each). 
* Logarithm: the result has the same number of decimal places as 
the number of significant figures in the argument. 
Forexample, log(1.234) = 0.0913 (four decimal places). 
Uncertainties are often recorded along with the measured values. Typically, 
uncertainties are rounded to one sf. For example, the length of the object 
in figure 29 can be recarded as 3.67 cm = 0.01 cm or (3.67 = 0.07) cm. 
Similarly, the mass of the sample from the previous page can be recorded as 
2.500g + 0.00Tg or (2.500 + 0.001)g. 
The discussion of precision, uncertainties and significant figures will continue 
in the next section.

The precision of a measured 
value must correspond to that of 
its uncertainty. In other words, 
the value itself should have the

as the uncertainty associated with 
it. For example, the expression

the precision of the value (one

3.3 Processing uncertainties 
You should be able to: 
v understand the significance of uncertainties in raw and processed data 
v’ record uncertainties in measurements as a range (+) to an appropriate level of precision 
v propagate uncertainties in processed data, in calculations involving addition, subtraction, multiplication, 
division and (HL) exponents 
v express measurement and processed uncertainties — absolute, fractional (relative) and percentage - to an 
appropriate number of significant figures or level of precision 
v apply the coefficient of determination (R?) to evaluate the fit of a trend line or curve. 
Uncertainties 
Measurements are always inexact, and any experimentally determined 
value is uncertain. When the same measurement is repeated, the results 
vary slightly because of the instrument imprecision, human reaction time 
and small fluctuations in temperature, pressure and other external factors. 
These variations, known as random errors, can be quantified and expressed 
as the uncertainty of the measurement. Therefore, every value obtained 
experimentally or calculated from experimental data should be recorded 
along with its uncertainty, as was discussed in the previous section. 
The uncertainty of a measurement can be estimated in several ways (table 4). 
When different estimation methods produce different uncertainties, the 
highest value must be used. An underestimated uncertainty can invalidate the 
results of the entire experiment and lead to an erroneous conclusion, such 
as the “discovery” of a trend or correlation that does not exist in reality. For 
example, a series of measurements might show an increase in a solution pH 
over time. However, this apparent increase could be caused by large random 
errors that, by chance, lowered the instrument readings at the beginning of the 
experiment and raised the readings at the end. 
In some cases, the uncertainty is 
more important than the 
measured value. In forensic 
science, an uncertain result must 
be rejected, as it could lead to 
conviction of an innocent person.

The precision of a measured value must correspond to that of its uncertainty. 
In other words, the value itself should have the same number of decimal 
places as the uncertainty associated with it. For example, the expression 
2.160 g = 0.002 gshows that the third decimal place in the measured 
value 2.160 g is uncertain, so that value is shown with three decimal places 
(including the trailing zero). If the uncertainty were 0.02 ginstead of 0.002 g, 
the value would be rounded to two decimal places: 2.16 g+ 0.02g. 
Uncertainty of a measurement can be improved by reducing random errors, 
which can be achieved by increasing the number of trials, controlling external 
variables (such as temperature in the laboratory) or using more precise 
instruments. 
Uncertainties can be expressed in different formats: absolute, relative or 
percentage.

For example, the expression 2.160 g + 0.002 g from table 4 shows that the

Propagation of uncertainties 
The overall uncertainty of acalculated result is estimated by propagating the 
uncertainty introduced by each of the measurements. The way this is done 
depends on the type of calculation (see table 5 and the following example). 
When an addition or subtraction involves an exact value (a constant with no 
associated uncertainty), that value does not affect the absolute uncertainty of 
the final result. Similarly, an exact number in a multiplication or division does 
not affect the relative uncertainty of the result.

independent variables is often characterized by the coefficient of determination

predictable relationship). When the relationship is represented as a graph, the 
R?value describes the degree of scattering of the data points: the closer the R? 
value to 1, the closer the data points to the line of best fit (figure 30).

qualitative trends while drawn or plotted graphs can be used to predict

the horizontal axis (x-axis), and the dependent variable(s) on the vertical axis 
(y-axis). Each graph should have a descriptive caption and, optionally, a 
number that can be used as a reference.

Lines or curves of best fit 
Experimentally determined data points almost never fit a straight line exactly 
because their positions are affected by random errors. Therefore, the general 
trend in a graph is often represented by a line of best fit, which does not pass 
through every data point but lies as close to the points as possible. On paper, 
the line of best fit is usually drawn by hand using the best judgement of the 
researcher. In plotted graphs, the computer software calculates the exact 
position of the best-fit line using various statistical methods. In all cases, the 
resulting line has roughly the same number of data points on either side of it 
(figure 30). Non-linear relationships between variables can be represented by 
a curve of best fit, which is drawn or plotted in a similar way (figure 31). 
Lines or curves of best fit can be used to analyse scattered experimental data 
and predict unknown guantities through interpolation or extrapolation (see 
next page). In turn, the data analysis can be used to improve the theoretical 
model based on the experimental results, identify and exclude outliers, and 
develop a plan for further experiments.

Common features of graphs 
Detailed analysis of arelationship between variables is often based on various 
features of a graph, such as maxima and minima, gradients, intercepts and area 
below the curve. The meaning and significance of these features depend on 
the nature of variables represented in the graph. 
In the simplest case, the maximum and minimum of the curve show the 
range of change of the dependent variable, such as temperature of the 
reaction mixture during a calorimetry experiment (figure 33). In other cases, 
the maximum or minimum may be used to identify a certain property of the 
analysed sample, such as the colours of visible light absorbed and transmitted 
by that sample (figure 34).

ranges (figure 37). The height of each bar in a histogram shows how frequently

Pie charts, also known as circle charts, are circular diagrams that represent 
fractions or percentages of quantitative data as slices of varying size. The area 
of each slice is proportional to the contribution of aparticular constituent to 
the total quantity it represents. Pie charts provide an easy way to visualize and 
compare parts to a whole, for example, the relative abundances of individual 
gases in a mixture (figure 38).

uncertainties of measurements. Uncertainty bars emphasize the fact that each 
data point represents a range of values. Vertical error bars show the uncertainty 
of the y-axis variable while horizontal error bars show the uncertainty of the 
x-axis variable (figure 39).

For most reactions, the rate approximately doubles when temperature increases by 10 degrees, so your sketch should show an exponential increase of the rate with temperature:
The reaction is exothermic ( > 0), so at low temperatures K ≫ 1 and the equilibrium position is shifted almost completely to the right (towards the products). Therefore, the theoretical yield at low temperatures will be close to 100%, and the curve will be almost horizontal.
An increase in temperature will shift the equilibrium position to the left (towards reactants) and thus reduce the theoretical yield of ammonia, so the curve will go down.
At high temperatures, K ≪ 1, so the equilibrium position will be shifted almost completely to the left (towards the reactants). Therefore, the theoretical yield of ammonia will become close to zero, and the curve will flatten again:
To score full marks, your sketch does not have to show all features of this curve (any decreasing curve or line would be acceptable).
An increase in temperature will both increase the reaction rate and shift the equilibrium position to the left. The first effect will increase the practical yield while the second effect will decrease that yield. Initially, the first effect will be dominant (because the rate will increase exponentially). At a certain temperature, the rate will become so high that the equilibrium will be reached almost instantaneously. Any further increase in temperature will reduce the practical yield because the equilibrium position will shift further and further to the left. Therefore, the practical yield will first increase and then decrease, so the resulting curve will look like the curve in part (a) at the beginning and like the curve in part (b) at the end:
This example demonstrates how technological processes can be optimized: to maximize the practical yield, the synthesis of ammonia must be carried out at a certain temperature (which in turn depends on the pressure and concentrations of the reactants). The optimal reaction conditions (temperature, pressure and concentrations) can be determined using computer modelling and then applied to the actual synthetic procedure.
